title: How Greek builds slang: suffixes, prefixes, loans, elision

blocks.title: Αργκό με κανόνες: slang is built, not just borrowed
blocks.text:
Greek slang can feel endless, but much of it comes from a small toolkit of suffixes and prefixes that every native speaker uses on the fly. Once you know the toolkit, you can understand words you have never heard before (*θεογκόμενα*, *ψιλοβαριέμαι*, *κωλοδουλειά*, *τυπάρας*) and, with care, coin your own.

The toolkit has seven parts, and this lesson takes them in order:

1. **Diminutives** (-άκι, -ούλα, -ίτσα, -ούλης, -άκος, -ουδάκι…): small, cute, affectionate, or belittling.
2. **Augmentatives** (-άρα, -αρος, -άρας, -αράς, -ούκλα, -α): big, impressive, or crude.
3. **Intensifying prefixes** (θεο-, κατα-, ολο-, παν-, ξε-, παρα-, τρισ-, σούπερ, μέγα/μεγαλο-) and the softener **ψιλο-**.
4. **Pejorative prefixes** (παλιο-, κωλο-, ψωρο-, βρομο-, χαζο-).
5. **Verb loans** in **-άρω** (τσεκάρω, παρκάρω, γκουγκλάρω, φλεξάρω…) and how they conjugate.
6. **Character and sensation suffixes**: -ιάρης, -άς/-ακλάς, -άκιας, -τζής, -ίλα, -ούρα, -μάρα.
7. **Speech shortcuts**: clipping, reduplication, onomatopoeia, and the elisions that make spoken Greek fast (τα 'φαγα, θα 'ρθω, μου 'πε, πού 'σαι, σ' αγαπώ).

The key point for a learner is **evaluation**. In Greek a suffix rarely changes only size: it adds an attitude. *Σπιτάκι* can be a cosy little house or a sneer at a tiny flat; *γιατρουδάκι* is not a small doctor but a doctor you do not rate. The tables mark the attitude in the *Meaning / nuance* column and give strength on the 0-5 scale (0 neutral, 1 casual, 2 slangy/cheeky, 3 rude, 4 vulgar).

blocks.text:
**Affectionate or belittling?**

The same suffix can stroke or stab. The deciding factors are the noun and the tone.

**Affectionate:** objects of comfort (καφεδάκι, ουζάκι, σπιτάκι), family (μανούλα, παππούλης), children and pets (γατούλα), and food offered as hospitality (*Φάε ένα κομματάκι!*). Diminutives here soften requests: *ένα νεράκι, παρακαλώ*, *ένα λεπτάκι*. Waiters, grandmothers and shopkeepers use them constantly.

**Belittling (1-2):** jobs, roles and adult people. **γιατρουδάκι** (a doctor not worth much), **υπαλληλάκος** (a petty clerk), **ανθρωπάκος** (a nobody), **δουλίτσα** (a cushy little number), **κυριούλα** (a frumpy, small-minded middle-aged woman), **γυναικούλα** (a woman who is petty or timid, sexist), **πολιτικάκος**, **ποιητάκος** (a two-bit politician or poet). Calling your boss *προϊσταμενάκος* is an insult.

**Irony:** *Έβγαλε κάτι λεφτουδάκια* can mean *he made a tidy sum*: the diminutive understates. *Ένα θεματάκι* is often a big problem.

blocks.title: How augmentatives behave
items: Most augmentatives become **feminine in -άρα** whatever the gender of the base: ο κώλος → η κωλάρα, το σπίτι → η σπιταρόνα, η φωνή → η φωνάρα.
Masculine **-άρας** (τυπάρας) and **-αρος** (παίδαρος) apply to men and carry admiration. **-αράς** with final stress (Ελληναράς, υπναράς) is a person defined by excess, usually mocked.
Youth speech uses **-άρα** as pure praise for nearly anything: *ταινιάρα, σειράρα, βραδιάρα, φωνάρα, τυπάρα* (of a woman). Spoken as an exclamation with no verb: **Ταινιάρα!** = What a film!
With body parts and women the same suffix turns crude (γκομενάρα, κωλάρα, βυζάρες): 3 at least, and in mixed company it reads as sexist.
Augmentatives are stressed on the suffix: φω**νά**ρα, τυ**πά**ρας, Ελλη**να**ράς, σπιτα**ρό**να. Get the stress wrong and you will not be understood.

blocks.text:
**ψιλο- is a social tool**

Greeks use **ψιλο-** to soften whatever might sound rude or demanding: *ψιλοβιάζομαι* (I'm in a bit of a hurry, so let's wrap up), *ψιλοκουράστηκα* (I'm kind of tired, so I'm leaving), *ψιλοθύμωσα* (I was a bit annoyed, which really means I was annoyed). Note the spelling: **ψιλο-** with ι (from ψιλός *fine, thin*), not ψηλο- (*tall*), although the two sound the same.

blocks.title: Pejorative prefixes: rules of thumb
items: The prefix attaches to almost any noun, and to some adjectives and verbs, so you can coin new words on the spot: *κωλοπρίντερ* (this bloody printer), *παλιοκίνητο* (this lousy phone). Natives do it constantly.
Strength scale: **παλιο- (1-2) < ψωρο-, βρομο- (2) < κωλο- (3) < σκατο- (3-4)**. With people the strength goes up a notch: παλιόπαιδο can be half-affectionate, κωλόπαιδο is an insult.
Aimed at objects and weather they are safe among friends; aimed at a person present they are insults. *Αυτό το κωλοπρίντερ* is fine at the office coffee machine, *ο κωλοδιευθυντής* is not.
Stress usually moves to keep the compound stress rule (stress on the antepenult or later): παλιό-καιρος → **παλιόκαιρος**, κωλο-παιδί → **κωλόπαιδο** (neuter in -ο), καιρός → **βρομόκαιρος**.
Linking vowel **-ο-** is fixed: κωλ-**ο**-δουλειά, ψωρ-**ο**-κακόμοιρος. Before a vowel, παλιο- usually drops it: παλι-άνθρωπος → **παλιάνθρωπος** (a scoundrel, now a word of its own).

blocks.title: Προφορά: stress and sound in derived slang
blocks.text:
**Suffixes carry the stress.** Almost every evaluative suffix pulls the stress onto itself: σπί-τι → σπι-**τά**-κι, γά-τα → γα-**τού**-λα, φω-**νή** → φω-**νά**-ρα, τύ-πος → τυ-**πά**-ρας, Έλ-λη-νας → Ελ-λη-να-**ράς**. If you keep the old stress the word sounds wrong. The diminutive -άκι makes the noun neuter and changes its plural: τα σπιτάκια, τα καφεδάκια (καφές → καφεδ-).

**Prefix compounds have one stress.** θεός + κουφός = **θεόκουφος** (THE-o-ku-fos), not two stresses. κατα- compounds keep the stress within the last three syllables: κατα**κόκ**κινος, κα**τά**μαυρος, κα**τά**κοπος. Learn them as whole words.

**-άρω verbs jump in the aorist and imperative.** τσε-**κά**-ρω, but **τσέ**-κα-ρα, **τσέ**-κα-ρε. With the -ισα aorist the stress stays: τσε-**κά**-ρι-σα. The double consonants of loans are single in Greek: κουλάρω (ku-LA-ro), not *kool*.

**Elision makes words fuse.** *Τα 'φαγα* is two syllables plus one: **TA-fa-gha**. *Θα 'ρθω* is **thar-tho**. *Πού 'σαι* is **PU-se**, with the stress on πού kept because it is the question word. *Σ' αγαπώ* is **sa-gha-PO**: three syllables, not four. In writing, the apostrophe marks the lost vowel. Never write *ταφαγα* or *θαρθω* except in casual Greeklish chat.

**Intonation of evaluation.** Augmentative praise is an exclamation: **Ταινιάρα!** with a high pitch on -ά- and a fall. Diminutive requests are soft and rising: *Ένα καφεδάκι;* Pejorative prefixes are spat out with extra stress and a little pause before the noun: *αυτή η… κωλο**δου**λειά*.

blocks.title: Η χώρα των υποκοριστικών: a culture of diminutives
blocks.text:
Visitors notice quickly that Greeks diminutise everything: **καφεδάκι, ουζάκι, μεζεδάκι, νεράκι, λεπτάκι, βολτίτσα, μπανάκι**. This is not baby talk. It is a politeness strategy: the diminutive makes an offer or a request feel small and easy to accept. *Θα πάρεις ένα γλυκάκι;* is harder to refuse than *Θα πάρεις γλυκό;*, and *Περίμενε ένα λεπτάκι* sounds friendlier than *περίμενε ένα λεπτό*. Shopkeepers, waiters and grandmothers are its masters.

The same habit has a sharp edge. Greek political and social commentary is full of belittling diminutives: **πολιτικάκος**, **δημοσιογραφίσκος**, **υπαλληλάκος**, **ανθρωπάκος**. Calling someone by a diminutive of their title strips their authority in one syllable.

**Ψωροκώσταινα**, from the scabby Kostaina, is the nickname Greeks give their own country when it seems poor, ridiculous or pretentious. It is self-mocking and loving at the same time, and you will meet it in op-eds and at kitchen tables alike. **Ελληναράς** is the matching portrait of a type: loud, proudly ignorant and rule-breaking, with no helmet, triple-parked and sure of himself. Greeks use it to criticise their own, so as a foreigner tread carefully.

The **-άρω** loans are older than the internet: **παρκάρω, φλερτάρω, κοπιάρω, σαλτάρω** came from Italian and French generations ago. The same template now absorbs English almost overnight: *γκουγκλάρω, ποστάρω, φλεξάρω, μπανάρω*. Language purists complain; everyone else conjugates.

**Common mistakes and false friends**

**σπιταρόνα ≠ homebody.** It is a huge house. A homebody is **σπιτόγατος / σπιτόγατα**.

**ψιλο- ≠ ψηλο-.** ψιλοβαριέμαι (a bit bored), not *ψηλοβαριέμαι*. ψηλός = tall.

**κατα- and θεο- are not freely stackable with everything.** *κατακόκκινος, θεόκουφος* are set; *κατα-καλός* does not exist. For ad hoc intensifying use **πάρα πολύ** or **σούπερ**.

**Diminutive ≠ small.** *Ένα θεματάκι* (a little issue) is often a real problem; *λεφτουδάκια* can be good money. Read the tone.

**γκομενάρα, κωλάρα** are not compliments you pay to a woman's face unless you know her well: 2-3 and sexist in most settings. **φωνάρα, ταινιάρα, τυπάρας** are fine.

**τσέκαρα, not *τσεκάρα*.** In the aorist and imperative the stress moves back: τσέκαρα, πάρκαρε, κούλαρε.

**κωλο- is rude (3).** It is fine for cursing at a printer, but not for a colleague's work. Use **παλιο-** for a milder grumble.

**Do not elide in writing formal Greek.** *Θα 'ρθω* is right in a text message, wrong in an email to a university.

blocks.title: Πού 'σαι, κολλητάρι;
blocks.text:
Μηνύματα στο κινητό, Παρασκευή απόγευμα

Δανάη: Πού 'σαι, κολλητάρι; Τι κάνεις απόψε;

Ηλίας: Τίποτα. Ψιλοβαριέμαι. Είμαι κατάκοπος από τη δουλειά, το κωλοπρόγραμμα κράσαρε πάλι και τα 'χασα όλα.

Δανάη: Άσ' το, μη γκρινιάζεις. Έχω μια ιδέα: πάμε σε ένα ταβερνάκι στην Πλάκα; Κάτι μεζεδάκια, ένα ουζάκι, μια βολτίτσα μετά.

Ηλίας: Ψιλοψήνομαι. Ποιοι θα 'ρθουν;

Δανάη: Η Μαρίνα, ο Στέλιος κι ένας φίλος του από τη Θεσσαλονίκη. Λένε ότι είναι τυπάρας και παίζει κιθάρα. Φωνάρα, λέει!

Ηλίας: Πω πω, ο Στέλιος πάλι με τους φιλαράκους του. Θυμάσαι εκείνον τον φιγουρατζή που φλέξαρε όλο το βράδυ το ρολόι του;

Δανάη: Χαχα, ναι, ο μεγαλοεπιχειρηματίας! Δεν είναι αυτός. Αυτός είναι παίδαρος, στο 'πα.

Ηλίας: Μου 'πε η Μαρίνα ότι ο Στέλιος έχει γίνει σπασίκλας τελευταία, όλο διαβάζει.

Δανάη: Ναι, ψιλοκαταλαβαίνω γιατί, έχει εξετάσεις. Αλλά απόψε θα κουλάρει, μου το υποσχέθηκε.

Ηλίας: Καλά, καλά. Πάντως εγώ δεν έχω λεφτουδάκια, είμαι στο μείον μέχρι την πληρωμή.

Δανάη: Κερνάω εγώ, μην ανησυχείς. Πήρα ένα μπονουσάκι αυτόν τον μήνα.

Ηλίας: Να 'σαι καλά! Και ο καιρός; Είδα ότι θα κάνει βρομόκαιρο.

Δανάη: Θα ψιλοβρέξει, λέει. Πάρε την ομπρελίτσα σου και μην είσαι μαμάκιας.

Ηλίας: Μαμάκιας εγώ; Θα 'ρθω τσακ-μπαμ! Αλλά πες μου την αλήθεια: θα 'ναι κι η Μαρίνα, ε;

Δανάη: Ναι… Γιατί; Μήπως έχεις καψούρα;

Ηλίας: Όχι, ρε! Απλώς ρωτάω.

Δανάη: Σιγά σιγά θα το παραδεχτείς. Το βλέπω απ' το πώς κοκκινίζεις. Γίνεσαι κατακόκκινος κάθε φορά που τη βλέπεις!

Ηλίας: Τι χαζομάρα. Τέλος πάντων. Στις εννιά στο Μοναστηράκι;

Δανάη: Στις εννιά. Και μην αργήσεις, γιατί θα σε γράψω στα παλιά μου τα παπούτσια!

Ηλίας: Το 'χω. Τα λέμε, κουκλίτσα.
blocks.en:
Text messages, Friday afternoon

Danai: Where are you, best mate? What are you doing tonight?

Ilias: Nothing. I'm kind of bored. I'm shattered from work, the bloody program crashed again and I lost everything.

Danai: Forget it, don't moan. I've got an idea: shall we go to a little taverna in Plaka? A few small dishes, a little ouzo, a little stroll afterwards.

Ilias: I'm sort of up for it. Who's coming?

Danai: Marina, Stelios and a friend of his from Thessaloniki. They say he's a legend and plays the guitar. Amazing voice, apparently!

Ilias: Oh no, Stelios again with his pals. Remember that show-off who flexed his watch all evening?

Danai: Haha, yes, the big-shot businessman! It isn't him. This one's a hunk, I told you.

Ilias: Marina told me Stelios has turned into a real swot lately, always studying.

Danai: Yeah, I sort of get why, he's got exams. But tonight he'll chill, he promised me.

Ilias: OK, OK. Anyway, I've got no cash, I'm in the red till payday.

Danai: My treat, don't worry. I got a little bonus this month.

Ilias: You're a star! And the weather? I saw it's going to be filthy.

Danai: It'll drizzle a bit, they say. Take your little umbrella and don't be a mummy's boy.

Ilias: Me, a mummy's boy? I'll be there in a flash! But tell me the truth: Marina will be there too, right?

Danai: Yes… Why? Have you got a crush?

Ilias: No, come on! I'm just asking.

Danai: You'll admit it eventually. I can see it from the way you blush. You go bright red every time you see her!

Ilias: What nonsense. Anyway. Nine o'clock at Monastiraki?

Danai: Nine. And don't be late, or I'll write you off!

Ilias: Got it. See you, sweetie.
